name: Cerium oxide

lead: Cerium oxide is a pale powder mostly used to polish glass and in catalysts. It has been suggested as a sunscreen ingredient because it absorbs UV with less photoreactivity than zinc or titanium oxide, which would suit products aimed at preventing sun-driven skin aging.

UV absorption comes from its semiconductor-like oxide lattice. Most research is on nanoparticle versions (nanoceria), which flip between Ce3+ and Ce4+ states and mimic antioxidant enzymes in the lab. No human trials of cerium oxide as a sunscreen or appearance product were found.

paras: It is a candidate ingredient in cosmetics discussions rather than a staple of mainstream sunscreens. Wikipedia describes nanoceria as a prospective replacement for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in sunscreens.
No human sunscreen trials were found. Laboratory work shows low cell toxicity in some models, but nanoparticle safety on skin has not been clinically established.

angle.text: Cerium oxide is discussed as a mineral UV absorber with lower photocatalytic activity than zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, which would suit sunscreens aimed at preventing skin aging. Antioxidant nanoceria research exists; human sunscreen studies do not.

lead: Cerium oxide (cerium(IV) oxide, ceria, CeO2) is a pale yellow-white, water-insoluble ceramic powder with a cubic fluorite crystal structure.[1] It is mainly an industrial material, used for glass polishing, glass decolourising, catalysts including automotive catalytic converters, and fuel cells.[1] In cosmetics discussions it appears as a candidate mineral UV absorber; Wikipedia describes nanoceria as a prospective replacement for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in sunscreens because of lower photocatalytic activity.[1]

Most of the scientific literature concerns cerium oxide nanoparticles (nanoceria) as redox-active materials that mimic antioxidant enzymes, and their toxicity. No human trials of cerium oxide as a sunscreen or appearance product were found.

paras: Cerium oxide is widely used for chemical-mechanical polishing of glass and optics (hobbyists call it opticians' rouge), to decolourise glass, in catalytic converters and oxidation catalysts, in solid oxide fuel cells and in welding electrodes.[1]

Nanoceria has been proposed as a sunscreen ingredient because it absorbs UV and shows lower photocatalytic activity than zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.[1] A comparative study of TiO2, ZnO and CeO2 nanoparticles found that the three differed in cellular toxicity mechanisms, with ZnO acting largely through dissolution and CeO2 showing low toxicity in the test system.[2]

Ceria readily and reversibly shifts between Ce3+ and Ce4+ states, forming oxygen-deficient lattices.[1] Nanoceria has been reported to mimic superoxide dismutase and catalase, with activity depending on the cerium redox state,[3][4] and its protein adsorption and cellular uptake depend on surface charge.[5] A review has discussed its pharmacological potential,[6] and a 2006 study reported that rare-earth nanoparticles prevented peroxide-induced retinal degeneration in rat cells.[7]

The 2008 comparative study reported that ZnO nanoparticles were toxic to cells through dissolution, whereas CeO2 was not, in the models used.[2] Wikipedia lists a low NFPA health rating for bulk cerium oxide and notes nanoceria has been investigated for antibacterial and antioxidant activity.[1] Safety of nanoceria applied to human skin has not been established by clinical studies found here.
No studies found. Research on cerium oxide nanoparticles to date is chiefly laboratory and animal work on antioxidant activity and toxicity, not clinical testing as a sunscreen.
